## Overview

Italians are an ethnic group and nation native to the Italian geographical region, sharing culture, history, ancestry and language. Approximately 55 million Italians live in Italy, representing 91% of the Italian national population; more than 5 million Italian citizens live outside Italy, while over 80 million people worldwide claim full or partial Italian ancestry. Italian-speaking groups are also found in Switzerland, France, Istria, Dalmatia and San Marino. Standard Italian is a Romance language of the Indo-European family that developed from Vulgar Latin. Italians are associated with regionalism and municipalism, and have influenced arts, music, science, technology, fashion, cinema, cuisine, sports, jurisprudence, banking and business.

## Material culture

### Architecture

The sources describe Italian cities as centers of political life, banking and foreign trade. From the 11th century onward, cities including Florence, Rome, Genoa, Milan, Pisa, Siena and Venice developed considerable independence; many became nearly independent city-states and maritime republics, each with its own foreign policy and trade.

## Music & performance

The sources state that Italians have influenced and contributed to music. They also state that the Renaissance began in Florence in the 14th century and led to a flourishing of the arts, literature, music and science. Italian cities, including Florence, Rome, Genoa, Milan, Pisa, Siena and Venice, were important centers of political life, banking and foreign trade. No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription is supplied for this country.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe several political and religious events in Italian history. Christianity became the Roman state religion in AD 380 under Emperor Theodosius I. Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne the Roman Emperor in 800, and the Papal States were established in central Italy in 756. On 2 June 1946, Italy held its first free election after more than 20 years of Fascist rule, and Italians chose to replace the monarchy with a republic.

## Foodways

The sources identify cuisine and restaurants as fields to which Italian people have contributed.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources mention literature as one of the fields that flourished during the Renaissance, which began in Florence in the 14th century. They also record legends and historical accounts concerning the name of Italy. The Latin name “Italia” may have been borrowed through Greek from the Oscan *Víteliú*, glossed as “land of calves.” Accounts by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Aristotle and Thucydides connect this etymology with the legend that Italy was named after the legendary King Italus.

## Language & religion

Standard Italian is a Romance language of the Indo-European language family that evolved from Vulgar Latin. Many Italian nationals also speak regional or minority languages native to Italy, and the sources state that UNESCO identifies approximately 30 languages native to Italy, although many are incorrectly called “Italian dialects.” The Latin terms *Italicus* and *Italianus* were used historically for inhabitants or people of Italy. In antiquity, inhabitants of Italy included Latins, Sabines, Etruscans, Greeks, Ligures, Celts, Sardinians and other peoples. Christianity became the Roman state religion in AD 380.
